titre: A Sound Emitted Near Heard Island, Picked Up in Bermuda and Washington State
accroche: In January 1991, coded signals emitted in the southern Indian Ocean were monitored at 16 sites, from both Atlantics to both Pacifics.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 1991, a research vessel, the Cory Chouest, with the help of the U.S. Navy, lowers acoustic sources near Heard Island, in the southern Indian Ocean. They emit coded signals at 57 hertz, a low frequency. What the researchers want to know is simple to state: will these signals be heard on the other side of the world?

## An Invisible Pipe in the Water

The answer comes down to a physical fact. Near the surface, temperature is the dominant factor in the speed of sound in the ocean. Going down, the water cools and sound slows. Farther down, pressure becomes the strongest influence, and sound speeds up again. Between the two, the speed passes through a minimum, at the base of the thermocline: this is the axis of the SOFAR channel, from the English "sound fixing and ranging." It lies at about 750 meters north of Hawaii, about 1,200 meters near Perth and Bermuda.

Sound always bends toward the layers where it travels most slowly. A wave that moves away from the axis is therefore sent back toward it, from both sides. Low frequencies especially stay trapped in this duct, without touching the surface or the bottom, where the rays would lose their energy. Sound can travel thousands of kilometers.

## From Lifeboat to Planetary Thermometer

The channel was described in the 1940s, independently, by Maurice Ewing and J. Lamar Worzel at Columbia, and by Leonid Brekhovskikh at the Lebedev Physical Institute. In 1944, Ewing and Worzel hang a hydrophone from the sailing ship Saluda while a second ship detonates charges up to 900 nautical miles away, about 1,700 kilometers. A military application: a SOFAR charge served as a distress signal for pilots, located thanks to differences in arrival time at listening stations.

The 1991 experiment aims at something else. It tests whether signals can cross ocean basins while keeping their phase, a prerequisite for a program of acoustic thermometry of ocean climate (ATOC): since the speed of sound depends on temperature, travel time is an indicator of it. The signals are monitored at 16 sites, in both Atlantics, both Pacifics, the Indian Ocean, and the Southern Ocean, and the conclusion is that phase-coherent processing is possible. The signal was notably picked up in Bermuda, in the North Atlantic, and at Whidbey Island, in Washington State, on the Pacific. At Ascension Island, 9,200 kilometers away, the signal-to-noise ratio is 19 to 30 decibels, judged surprisingly high, for a travel time of about 1 hour 44 minutes.

## What This Changes

The shift comes down to an inversion: the ocean, opaque to sight, is a waveguide for sound. A travel time then becomes a possible measure of temperature over thousands of kilometers. The test also raised a question: would this noise disturb marine mammals? The observers noted no sign of distress. On the equipment side, most of the sources broke down during the campaign. Low sounds attributed to fin whales are frequent in the channel, and these whales might use it to communicate with other fin whales many kilometers away: whom are they talking to, and how far?

quiz.question: Why does a low sound emitted in the SOFAR channel carry so far?
choix: It is sent back by refraction toward the channel axis, without touching the surface or the bottom
It bounces off the seafloor, which reflects it almost without loss
It travels at constant speed regardless of depth, without being deflected
It is amplified by the thermocline, which acts as a loudspeaker
quiz.explication: Sound bends toward the layers where it is slowest: the channel axis. Low frequencies stay trapped there, away from the surfaces where they would lose their energy. Rays that touch the bottom or the surface lose energy, and the speed of sound is not constant: it passes through a minimum.

Johannes Schmidt in Denmark and Walter Munk in the United States
Jacques-Yves Cousteau in France and Alfred Wegener in Germany
Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace in England
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The channel was described in the 1940s, independently, by Maurice Ewing and J. Lamar Worzel at Columbia, and by Leonid Brekhovskikh at the Lebedev Physical Institute.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At how many sites were the signals emitted near Heard Island in January 1991 monitored, and where?
choix: At only 2 sites, in Bermuda and Australia
At 16 sites, from both Atlantics to both Pacifics, the Indian Ocean, and the Southern Ocean
At a single site, on Ascension Island
At 100 sites spread across all the continents
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The signals were monitored at 16 sites, in both Atlantics, both Pacifics, the Indian Ocean, and the Southern Ocean, to test whether phase-coherent processing was possible over these distances.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the 1991 Heard Island test meant to serve, beyond the simple propagation of sound?
choix: To locate schools of fish for commercial fishing
To detect enemy submarines during the Cold War
To map the underwater volcanoes of the Indian Ocean
To prepare a program of acoustic thermometry of ocean climate, temperature influencing the speed of sound
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1991 experiment aimed to test whether signals could cross ocean basins while keeping their phase, a prerequisite for a program of acoustic thermometry of ocean climate, the speed of sound depending on temperature.
